task.goal: Keep an unattended reading corner in a public waiting room tidy and welcoming without turning volunteers into full-time monitors.
hard_constraints: One shelf, donated books and two 15-minute volunteer visits per week.
No camera, user registration, fines or public naming of borrowers.
Check availability, condition, cleanup effort and access for seated readers.
task.available_resources: Printable shelf guides and a nearby return box.
task.expected_result: A self-maintaining borrowing ritual and small pilot.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Return first, then choose
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: give every borrowed book the same easy return route, so readers need not understand shelving or judge condition. A printable guide says: “Choose a book. Read here or take it away. When finished, put it in the return box. No sign-up or deadline.” Add: “Please return books with loose pages or spills too; volunteers will check them.” This separates browsing from returned material and gives volunteers one predictable place to work.

Use the shelf for upright, readable books with visible titles and comfortable gaps. Locate the existing return box beside it, outside circulation space and within seated reach where possible. A seated reader should be able to read the guide, choose several books and return one without standing. If the shelf configuration prevents that, concentrate the usable selection in its reachable section; placement alone may not provide independent access for everyone.

Each of the two weekly 15-minute visits follows the same order: clear any obstruction, inspect returns for dampness, sharp staples or loose pages, reshelve usable books, straighten the selection, and count available books. Pause additional donation intake if it would crowd the shelf. The host must agree on where unsuitable books go; do not quietly accumulate a second pile.

The outcome changes through reduced decision-making and concentrated cleanup. It assumes readers notice the guide, the box can hold returns between visits, and the host permits take-home borrowing. It cannot guarantee returns or prevent depletion. The shelf remains welcoming only while borrowing losses and donations roughly balance.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Run a four-week pilot, using the first week with ordinary shelving and a basic borrowing notice as the comparator, then introduce the return-first guide. At every visit, record available usable books, damaged books mixed into the selection, misplaced books, box overflow and minutes needed to restore order. Check reach and legibility with a willing seated reader. Treat the mechanism as unsupported if cleanup does not become easier, the box repeatedly overflows, or fewer usable books remain accessible. This small sequential comparison can expose failure but cannot establish causation because traffic and donations may vary.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Visible spaces invite readers to reset the shelf
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: make the tidy state obvious and easy to restore immediately. Printable shelf guides divide the reachable shelf into a few broad, plainly labelled areas, such as “Stories,” “Facts” and “Short reads.” Avoid detailed cataloguing. Leave visible gaps so replacing a book is physically easy. A guide says: “Borrow freely. Finished here? Put it back in its labelled space. Unsure where it belongs, or found damage? Use the return box.”

Readers perform a small reset at the moment they finish, spreading routine tidying across use instead of reserving it for volunteers. The nearby box acts as an escape route when classification or condition is uncertain. Unlike mandatory box returns, this arrangement lets usable books become available again immediately.

At each of the two 15-minute weekly visits, volunteers inspect the shelf and return box, remove unsuitable books through a host-approved route, restore category boundaries and count readable books. Fit the labels to the actual donated collection rather than promising categories with no books. Keep all reachable sections lightly filled, with readable spines and enough clearance to grasp a book while seated. Do not occupy walking or wheelchair space with overflow. New donations enter only when space exists.

This requires a shelf that can display clear boundaries and readers who can interpret a few simple labels. Large print and plain language reduce barriers, but do not eliminate language, vision or mobility barriers. The principle is environmental feedback: an obvious destination and visible spare space reduce the effort of putting something away. Its main limitation is that readers may reshelve damaged books or ignore categories; volunteers still provide the condition check. Classification must remain optional rather than becoming a new burden on borrowers.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare one week of an unpartitioned shelf with three weeks of labelled spaces, keeping borrowing permissions unchanged. At each visit, record cleanup minutes, books lying outside the shelf, usable books available and condition problems found among shelved books. Ask a willing seated reader to select and replace a book, noting reach or label difficulties. Reject or simplify the arrangement if category correction consumes the saved cleanup time, damage becomes harder to detect, or readers cannot readily replace books. Counts describe this corner only; changes in visitor numbers remain an uncertainty.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Keep a small reading reserve and circulate the rest
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: protect a small amount of reliable on-site availability while allowing the remainder to circulate freely. Divide the single shelf with printable guides into “Read here—leave here for the next reader” and “Take a book—bring it back when finished.” Put a modest selection of appealing, short or easily browsed donated books in the first section. Both sections must include books reachable from a seated position; the protected selection must not occupy all the accessible space.

The ritual is: choose either section, return an on-site book to its section after reading, and place take-home returns or damaged books in the nearby box. Use friendly instructions without monitoring, registration, penalties or borrower identification. An on-site label is a request, not an enforceable restriction. Anyone may still remove those books, so availability is buffered rather than guaranteed.

During each of the two weekly 15-minute visits, volunteers check both sections and the box for condition, clear obstructions, count usable books and restore the small on-site selection from suitable donations already available. Keep the total stock loose enough for easy selection and replacement. Agree with the host on disposal or removal of unusable donations before starting; refuse overflow rather than creating floor piles.

This changes the outcome by separating immediate reading availability from take-home circulation. It assumes the host accepts two borrowing permissions, enough suitable donated books exist, and readers can distinguish the signs. It is useful where a fully circulating collection often disappears between visits. The tradeoff is extra instruction and a possible perception that the best books cannot be borrowed. Reserve only a small share and explain the shared benefit. It does not inherently reduce litter or damage, so the reset ritual and short volunteer inspection remain necessary.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use an all-circulating shelf for one week, then the split arrangement for three weeks. At every visit, record usable books in each section, total cleanup minutes, condition problems and any apparent confusion about returns. Have a willing seated reader demonstrate choosing from both sections and returning a book. The proposal fails its practical purpose if the on-site section repeatedly empties, accessible choice declines, or sorting takes longer without improving availability. Sparse observations cannot establish how often the shelf was empty between visits; report that limitation explicitly.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Borrow a book, give the corner a ten-second reset
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: invite each borrower to perform one optional act of care for the whole corner, including books they did not use. A printable guide says: “Enjoy a book here or take one home. If you can, leave the corner a little nicer: straighten one fallen book or put one damaged book in the return box. One small action is enough. Borrowing is always welcome.” This makes borrowing an occasion for shared upkeep, without assigning anyone a monitoring role.

Unlike simply asking readers to replace their own books, the invitation addresses disorder left by previous visitors. It could work if even a minority of readers complete a useful action. The contribution must remain optional: readers who cannot reach, handle books or spare time have equal permission to borrow.

Use the single shelf, donated books, one large-print guide and the nearby return box. Keep an uncrowded selection within seated reach, with readable titles and room to grasp books. Label the box for returns and books needing attention; ask readers to flag obvious damage rather than repair or clean it. Volunteers handle condition decisions. Before starting, agree with the host on a removal route for unusable books so the box does not become permanent storage.

At each of the two weekly 15-minute visits, volunteers clear access, inspect returns and shelved books, restore usable stock and record the shelf’s state before tidying. Include recording within the time limit.

The necessary assumptions are that visitors notice the invitation and enough are willing and able to help. The main uncertainty is whether this produces useful care or merely adds signage. It cannot ensure returns, prevent depletion or replace volunteer inspection.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Run a four-week pilot. Alternate weeks between a simple borrowing-and-return notice and the same notice with the optional ten-second reset invitation. Keep stock placement and volunteer routines consistent. At each visit, record usable books available, fallen or displaced books, condition problems, return-box overflow and cleanup minutes. Ask a willing seated reader to demonstrate choosing and returning a book and interpreting the invitation; check that helping feels optional. Drop the invitation if cleanup does not improve, available books decline, or it creates pressure or access difficulties. Eight observations can expose practical failure but cannot establish causation or reveal availability between visits.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Let the return reminder travel with the book
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: move the return cue from the shelf to the place where readers finish reading. Offer small, folded printable guides that double as bookmarks: “Taking this book home? Take a reminder. When finished, bring both back to the reading corner’s return box. No deadline or sign-up.” Include the waiting room’s recognizable location. Readers place a guide inside their chosen book; volunteers recover and reuse clean guides from returns.

The intended change is fewer forgotten books and more predictable replenishment. A shelf notice disappears from view after departure; a bookmark can reappear during reading and at completion. This differs from asking readers to tidy: it supports remembering a future action. Participation stays optional, and borrowing never depends on taking a guide.

Use only the single shelf, donated books, printable guides and nearby return box. Fold one printed guide into a shallow holder for the others, within seated reach. Keep the borrowing instruction visible on the shelf as well. Avoid book identifiers, borrower details, return dates or tracking codes. Provide a loose selection with grasping space and readable titles in the shelf’s reachable section.

During each of the two weekly 15-minute visits, volunteers inspect books and returns, restore usable stock, replenish reminders and remove loose paper. Record observations within that allowance. Agree beforehand on a host-approved destination for unusable books; accept donations only when shelf capacity permits.

This assumes take-home borrowing is allowed, readers can identify and revisit the location, and printing includes small take-away guides. It may improve returns without changing immediate browsing disorder. Guides could be ignored, lost or become litter; books may still disappear. The corner must remain usable without a bookmark.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot for four weeks: two with a shelf-only borrowing notice, then two with the same wording offered as portable reminders. At each visit, record usable books available, returned books, condition problems, loose paper, box overflow and total cleanup minutes. Note incoming donations separately. Ask one willing seated reader to choose a book, obtain a reminder and use the return box. Reject the mechanism if reminders create clutter or extra work without any encouraging return or availability signal. Delayed returns, changing traffic and only eight observations limit inference; this check can reveal practical failure, not establish an effect on return rates.

EXPAND.title: Let books travel onward without requiring a return
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: remove the return obligation entirely. The shelf becomes a free book exchange: “Read here or take a book. Keep it, pass it on, or return it when convenient. No replacement needed.” This eliminates a coordination step that a welcoming reading corner does not necessarily require. Readers who cannot revisit can still participate without leaving an unfinished obligation.

Use one printable guide on the shelf and label the nearby box “Book contributions and optional returns.” Keep readable donated books loosely arranged, with a useful choice within seated reach. The box must also be reachable without blocking circulation. Readers choose, read or take, and optionally contribute later; nobody records individual transactions.

One named volunteer owns the pilot, with either volunteer following the same routine during the two weekly 15-minute visits: clear access, inspect the box and shelf, remove unusable material through an agreed host route, replenish from usable contributions, and count available books. Stop accepting contributions when the shelf and box cannot safely contain them. Do not create extra storage or collection duties.

The changed causal link is participation without an expected return journey. Compared with the prior return-first route, this could reduce books waiting elsewhere to be returned and encourage onward sharing, but it could also accelerate depletion. It assumes the host permits permanent removal and existing donations can support enough reading choice. There is no evidence here that either assumption holds. This route is unsuitable if maintaining the same collection is essential; its success depends on continued usable supply, not compliance with borrowing instructions.
EXPAND.experiment: The pilot owner runs two weeks with the prior return-first notice, then two weeks with the optional-return exchange, keeping starting stock approximately equal using only available donations. At every scheduled visit, record usable books available, condition defects, cleanup minutes and new contributions. Check guide visibility, choosing and returning with a willing seated reader during one visit. Stop early if no usable books remain, access is obstructed, or restoration exceeds 15 minutes twice. Retain the change only if availability remains acceptable to the host and cleanup improves without extra donation-seeking work. Visit counts cannot establish availability throughout the intervening days, and changing traffic limits the comparison.

EXPAND.title: Prevent unsuitable donations from entering the corner
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: control incoming material before it becomes cleanup work. Donated books can overwhelm a corner through poor condition, unsuitable formats or sheer volume even when borrowing and returning work well. Give new donations a simple acceptance gate during the existing volunteer visits instead of treating every deposited item as shelf stock.

With the host, print two recurring 15-minute donation windows matching the volunteer visits. The guide says: “Borrow freely; return borrowed books in the box. New donations: please bring one or two clean, dry, complete books during the times below, and wait while we check space.” No purchase or donation is required to borrow. Do not ask for donor names or retain contact details.

A volunteer accepts a donation only after checking condition and confirming that it fits on the single shelf without crowding the seated-reach selection. The donor retains anything declined. Keep the borrowing ritual simple: choose freely and put returns in the nearby box. At each visit, first clear access and inspect returns, then assess any offered donations and straighten the shelf. Donation assessment shares the same 15-minute limit; it does not extend the visit. Unexpected deposits still require a host-approved removal route rather than another pile.

Unlike the prior return-first route, this prevents some cleanup inputs rather than concentrating them for later sorting. It needs host agreement, predictable visit times and donors willing to wait briefly. It may substantially reduce useful supply or consume volunteer time in conversations. If excess or unsuitable donations are uncommon, the gate has little benefit and should not be retained. The owner should introduce it only after a short baseline confirms that incoming donations are a material source of work.
EXPAND.experiment: A named volunteer records two baseline weeks using the return-first arrangement, including unsuitable incoming books, usable availability and total cleanup time. Trial the donation gate for two further weeks without adding visits. Include acceptance conversations in the time total, and record unattended deposits and useful books declined for lack of space. During a scheduled visit, ask a willing seated reader to choose and return a book, checking reach and unobstructed access. Stop the gate if conversations prevent basic cleanup within 15 minutes twice, or usable stock falls below a host-agreed minimum at two consecutive visits. Reject it if reduced sorting is offset by intake work, reduced availability or more abandoned donations. This small comparison can expose those costs but cannot prove causation.

EXPAND.title: Return-box borrowing with a capacity fallback
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “Return first, then choose.” Preserve its simple ritual: choose a book, read here or borrow it, and return it through the nearby box so volunteers check condition before reshelving. The consequential gap is what readers should do when the box fills between visits; the source measures overflow but supplies no everyday response.

Add a printable fill line below the box opening and this instruction: “Return here while there is room below the line. If full, please keep your return until another visit. Please leave the floor and shelf clear.” This makes capacity a visible decision boundary without requiring a monitor. It shifts some waiting and carrying to returning readers; it may also delay books becoming available. It is worthwhile only if overflow is a credible problem.

One existing volunteer owns the pilot; either volunteer can perform the same two weekly 15-minute visits. Clear access first, then empty and inspect returns, remove unsuitable books through a host-agreed route, reshelve usable books and count availability. Handle books individually so an interrupted visit leaves no sorting pile: unchecked books remain in the box, checked books go directly onto the shelf. Pause new donations whenever they would consume the return capacity or crowd the shelf.

Keep readable titles, grasping space and a useful selection within seated reach. Put the guide and box within seated reach where the existing layout permits, without obstructing circulation. Before launch, the host must agree to borrowing and an unsuitable-book removal route. If the box cannot accommodate ordinary returns between visits, this arrangement is unsuitable: revert to a clearly labelled read-here-only corner until capacity or the permitted layout changes. That fallback sacrifices take-home borrowing but keeps reading available within the same resources. The instruction cannot guarantee compliance or prevent depletion.
EXPAND.experiment:
An existing volunteer runs a four-week pilot within the eight scheduled visits: one week with the basic return-first notice, then three with the fill line and fallback. Record usable books available, condition problems on the shelf and in returns, overflow or floor deposits, and total restoration minutes. During a scheduled visit, ask a willing seated reader to choose and return a book and interpret the full-box instruction; correct placement or wording immediately if needed.

If the box reaches the line at two consecutive visits, the owner pauses new donations. If overflow recurs after that change, or restoration exceeds 15 minutes twice, switch to the stated read-here-only fallback and inspect its availability and cleanup at the remaining visits. Retain take-home borrowing only if cleanup fits the visits, accessible choice remains acceptable to the host, and the capacity instruction is understandable. Compared with the source, the expected benefit is fewer abandoned returns; the shifted cost is delayed returns and possible lost availability. Visit observations cannot establish conditions throughout the week or show how many readers carried books away again.

EXPAND.title: Choose a book, rescue one stray
EXPAND.proposal:
New mechanism: use the existing moment of choosing a book to recruit a tiny amount of shared cleanup. Readers need not learn shelving or restore the entire corner. A printable guide says: “Choose freely—read here or borrow. Finished books go in the return box. If you notice one book left on a seat or table within easy reach, you can put it in the box too. One is enough; helping is optional.” Add: “Leave anything wet, sharp or visibly dirty for the volunteers.”

This removes the assumption that the person who leaves a book must be the person who restores order. Unlike category guides, its main action is recovering somebody else’s abandoned book, using an already occurring visit rather than adding a trip or reminder. Readers should not move books beside somebody’s belongings or interrupt an occupied seat. The invitation applies only to apparently abandoned books in the immediate corner; readers do not patrol the waiting room or handle general litter.

Use the single shelf, existing return box and printed guide. An existing volunteer owns the pilot. During each of the two weekly 15-minute visits, volunteers clear access, inspect rescued books and other returns, reshelve usable books, remove unsuitable material through a host-agreed route and straighten the shelf. Leave no sorting pile if interrupted. Keep the box below a printed fill line; the guide says to skip the optional rescue when it is full. Pause donation intake when space is insufficient.

Provide a useful selection and legible instructions within seated reach, with room to grasp books and approach the box. Participation never requires standing, reaching across other people or helping before borrowing. This assumes readers notice stray books and can distinguish abandoned material from somebody’s current reading. Compared with volunteer-only cleanup, it could shorten the time books remain scattered; the costs are extra reader effort, possible mistaken removal and more books awaiting inspection. If those costs appear, remove the rescue invitation and retain ordinary borrowing and volunteer cleanup.
EXPAND.experiment:
Run one baseline week with ordinary return-box borrowing, followed by three weeks with the optional rescue invitation. The owner records at each scheduled visit usable books available, books left around the corner, condition problems, return-box fullness and cleanup minutes. Do not record borrower identities. During one visit, ask a willing seated reader to interpret the instruction and demonstrate choosing and returning a book; check reach, guide visibility and whether the invitation feels optional.

Remove the rescue invitation immediately if a reader reports that an actively used book was taken, or if the invitation causes unsafe reaching. Remove it after two visits with overflow or cleanup exceeding 15 minutes. Continue only if scattered books decrease without unacceptable loss of shelf availability or added sorting work. Fewer stray books would support the practical result, but these observations cannot distinguish reader rescue from changes in traffic or ordinary borrower behavior.
